WHERE THE WAR IS AT

September 1940. The alliance with Germany and Italy is on the table, and the Southern Resource Area's oil and rubber sit behind every argument being made in this room right now. China is still unresolved after three years. What Tokyo does next, in each of these rooms, is yours to decide.

"To finish this war, our armies would need to march to Washington itself. I do not believe this nation is prepared for what that actually requires."

— YAMAMOTO

END OF HOSTILITIES: 1946
PACIFIC SITUATION — THE WAR ACTUALLY FOUGHT
Held to the Last Man, Lost to the Ledger
MAJOR DEFEAT
IMPERIAL GENERAL HEADQUARTERS, BEGINNING 1940
READINESS
-6
PIPELINE
-10
INITIATIVE
+3
A PLUS READING MEANS BETTER SUPPLIED AND RUNNING AHEAD OF SCHEDULE. A MINUS READING MEANS THE REVERSE.

Imperial Headquarters chose a war against the Soviet Union over a war against the United States: withdrew from Siberia once the winter made the gamble's cost clear, ran that delayed operation deliberately, spending time it couldn't fully spare, starving the Kwantung Army's own allocation to keep the Navy fueled. On balance, this was the harder road available to Tokyo in 1941. This staff declined to reckon with the cost in writing and pressed forward instead, the same unexamined momentum that let the original 1941 optimism go untested against Nomonhan's own lessons for as long as it did. The southern war fought two years late, on a ledger this command chose not to read, closes out anyway.

COUNCIL FOLLOWED

Most trusted advisor: Nagano (4 councils) · also heeded Tojo (3), Sugiyama (2)

VOICES NOT HEARD

Passed over most often: Tojo (6), Nagano (5)

THE DICE YOU ROLLED

This war passed through 1 contested outcome. The compound likelihood of the exact path you walked: ~70%. Portions of this path are marked speculative: the odds above are a statement of how far it stands from what the evidence supports.

COMMAND TIMELINE · 11 DIVERGENCES FROM THE RECORD
SCORECARD VS. HISTORY · MATCHED 2/4, OUT-POSITIONED 1/4
DECISION LOG
1940 — Escalate the military pressure while quietly keeping a back channel open: force better terms rather than choosing between war and peace
SEPTEMBER 1940 — Sign the Tripartite Pact, formalizing the alliance with Germany and Italy
LATE 1940 — Leave the services running parallel: unification fights are for peacetime, not for a staff about to plan a war
JULY 1941 — Execute Kantokuen: strike north into Siberia while Soviet attention is fixed on Germany
AUGUST 1941 — Limit the objective: seize the border regions and key resource areas, decline the deeper drive
1942 — Cut losses: negotiate a local ceasefire with Soviet forces and withdraw to the original border
1943 – 1944 — Proceed deliberately: apply the caution the Siberian front's own hard lessons argue for, despite the compounding fuel deficit
